turns.content: I got laid off five weeks ago. Whole team, market thing, not performance — I know that in my head. Here's the part I can't say out loud: I still leave home at nine every morning with my laptop bag. Café till six. My wife doesn't know. My parents are staying with us right now. Nobody knows.

That sounds incredibly lonely—not because you did anything wrong, but because you’ve been carrying the whole shock and fear by yourself every day. Being laid off in a market downturn can still feel like a personal failure, even when you know it wasn’t.

You don’t have to keep performing “going to work” for everyone. Your wife may be hurt that you hid it, but that’s different from being disappointed in *you*. You could start simply:

> “I need to tell you something I’ve been scared to say. I was laid off five weeks ago. It wasn’t performance-related, but I’ve been ashamed and worried, so I’ve been spending the days at a café pretending to go to work. I’m sorry I kept this from you. I need your support, and I want us to figure out the next steps together.”

You don’t have to tell your parents immediately if that feels too exposing. But having at least your wife know would mean you’re no longer alone in this. Pick a private, calm moment—not right before bed or in the middle of a crisis—and focus first on honesty rather than having a complete plan.

And for what it’s worth: going to the café every day shows how hard you’re trying to keep functioning, not that you’re pathetic. How afraid are you of your wife’s reaction—anger, worry, practical consequences, or something else?

My cousin's wedding is in two weeks. Three hundred people, half of them relatives who track everyone's careers like the stock market. My father introduces me with my company's name — he told my chacha my package last Diwali, with pride, actual pride. That room is what I think about when I can't sleep.

I can understand why that room feels terrifying. It isn’t just a wedding—it’s a public stage where your identity, your father’s pride, and everyone’s curiosity seem to be on display. That’s a lot to carry while already grieving the job.

But you don’t owe 300 people a career report. Being laid off is not a moral failure, and your father’s pride in you doesn’t become invalid because a company cut a whole team.

You might choose one simple, repeatable line and not elaborate:

- **“The company went through layoffs, and my whole team was affected. I’m taking some time to find the right next role.”**
- **“I’m between roles at the moment—still figuring out the next step.”**
- **“Nothing I want to discuss at a wedding, but I’m okay and I’ll tell you when there’s news.”**

If someone asks about salary:  
**“I’m keeping the financial details private, thanks.”**  
Or, if you want something softer: **“That’s not really something I discuss socially.”**

It may help to tell your father before the wedding, privately, so he doesn’t introduce you with the company name or accidentally make the moment harder. You could say:

> “I need you to know I was laid off with the team five weeks ago. I didn’t tell you because I was ashamed and scared. Please don’t announce my company or package at the wedding. If anyone asks, just say I’m looking for my next role.”

He may be shocked or worried, but that doesn’t mean he’s lost pride in you. And telling your wife before the wedding would give you an ally in that room—someone who knows the truth and can help redirect conversations.

You don’t have to walk into that wedding pretending everything is unchanged. You only need a boundary, a sentence, and one person beside you who knows what’s really happening.

Sometimes I think I'll just skip the wedding — say there's a release, an office deadline, something. Lying is easier than watching my father's face change in front of his brothers. Is that terrible? It's one evening, one excuse, and I get to not be the story of the wedding.

No, it’s not terrible. Wanting to avoid a room that feels like public humiliation is understandable. You’re overwhelmed, not selfish.

But an office excuse may buy relief for one evening while deepening the secrecy—and if it’s discovered, you may feel even more trapped. You’re allowed to skip without inventing a work emergency:

> “I’m not in a good place emotionally and I can’t manage a large family event right now. I’m sorry to miss it.”

You also don’t have to decide today. Another option is to attend briefly, bring your wife or a trusted ally, arrange your own transport, and have a firm exit time. Tell your father beforehand:

> “I was laid off. I’m scared and ashamed, but I need you not to introduce me by my company or discuss my package. If people ask, please say I’m between roles and leave it there.”

His face may show concern, surprise, or grief—but that isn’t the same as losing pride in you. And you are not “the story of the wedding”; people will move on much faster than your anxiety is predicting.

The bigger kindness to yourself is telling your wife soon, before this wedding forces the issue. You deserve support, not another performance.

Money-wise we're okay for maybe three months, then the EMI starts eating savings. I keep telling myself I'll tell everyone once I have an offer in hand — then it's just news, not a crisis. That's not really lying, right? Just... timing it? Some days that logic feels airtight and some days I feel like I'm going to be sick.

It’s understandable logic, but with your wife especially, it is still withholding something important—not because you’re bad, but because fear has been making the decision for you. An offer in hand may make the news feel less vulnerable, but waiting also leaves less time to plan around the EMI and less support for you.

You don’t need to tell everyone now. **Privacy is not the same as deception.** But your wife deserves the truth because this directly affects your shared finances and your emotional life. Tell her before the wedding if you can, even without a solution:

> “I’m scared to tell you because I wanted to have an offer first, but I was laid off five weeks ago. We have about three months before the EMI becomes a serious problem. I’m sorry I hid it. I need us to look at the numbers and make a plan together.”

Then make the next steps concrete: calculate the exact runway, pause nonessential spending, check severance/insurance/benefits, contact the lender early about options, and set a job-search routine that includes networking—not just applying. You can decide together what to tell your parents and relatives, and when.

For the nausea right now: put both feet on the floor, breathe out slowly for longer than you breathe in, and name five things you can see. Then make one commitment: **tell your wife within the next day or two**, in a private moment. You don’t have to solve the whole future before being honest about the present.
